svg.aria-label: Diagram: the four Cloud Audit Log types and which are configurable or chargeable, how the IAM permission type decides which log a method writes and therefore whether it is on by default, the exemption that stops publicly shared resources generating audit logs at all, and the retention periods that make organization-level auditing require a sink
svg.title: Auditing IAM: who granted what is always recorded; who read the policy is not
svg.text: Who granted a role is always recorded. Who read the policy is not.
The permission type decides which log a method writes, and that decides whether it is on by default.
Four log types, and the pattern hiding in the defaults
Type
Configurable
Chargeable
Admin Activity
No; always written
No
System Event
No; always written
No
Data Access
Yes — OFF by default
Yes
Policy Denied
Yes; excludable from buckets
Yes
The two you cannot turn off are the two that cost nothing. That is the whole shape.
The permission type decides the log type, and the log type decides the default
ADMIN_WRITE → Admin Activity: always written, cannot be disabled, free.
ADMIN_READ / DATA_READ / DATA_WRITE → Data Access: OFF by default, chargeable.
SetIamPolicy is ADMIN_WRITE. GetIamPolicy is ADMIN_READ.
So WHO GRANTED a role is always recorded. WHO READ the policy is not, unless you enabled it.
And one category of resource is exempt entirely
Publicly available resources with allUsers or allAuthenticatedUsers generate NO audit logs.
Nor does anything reachable without signing in. Google states the reason: it protects
end-user identities and information, a deliberate privacy trade rather than an oversight.
The consequence stands regardless: your most exposed resources are your least logged.
Retention, which is where organization-level auditing goes wrong
_Required (Admin Activity and System Event): 400 days, NOT configurable. Good by default.
_Default at FOLDER or ORGANIZATION: 30 days, also NOT configurable.
To keep org-level entries longer, route them with a sink into a project log bucket,
where retention is configurable from 1 day to 3650 days.
#48: the Service Agent Manager is visible ONLY in audit logs. #55: alert on SetIamPolicy().
#56: break-glass use looks like a login unless you built the rule. All three land here.
Entries are immutable, and Admin Activity survives even disabling the Logging API.
So the record of who changed access is the most trustworthy artifact in this series.
